For the auxiliary segmentation objective, did you use the masks generated by your 3D segmentation models as the ground truth labels? If so, does that mean you also added a decoder module to your classification models to predict segmentation masks?

Thank you, yes we used 3D segmentation models output as ground truth, while training classification models, along with linear classifier head, we used 1 / 2 separate mask heads/decoders. So, our loss function looks something like this.

Hey, congratulations on the win!
I had a few question:

  1. You mentioned using @Theviel's dataset processing code. I saw on their profile and the one that I found converts dcm to png. Did you guys also do it?
  2. >each volume extracted with equi-distant 96 slices.
    What does this mean? Let's say a study has 1000 slices, you'd pick a slice after every 96 slices? Also why did you do this?

Sorry for the basic questions, I am a noob trying to replicate your solution for understanding purposes.

Answer 1

Yes, Early in the competition we created our own dataset, we used it for a long time, near the end, we tried theo's public dataset, which results in similar scores to our own but the ensemble boost was relevant

Answer 2

For example, If a study has 1000 slices, then we make volumes by selecting (0-96), (96-192), (192-288) and so on… and then each volume will be given to the model to make predictions on, generally taking more slices than 96 might result in better performance but it also uses a lot of GPU memory

Sorry for asking the same kind of question again, but just to clarify, PNGs produced a better result than dicoms?

Also, did you use the nii files provided by the authors to do something?

No, it was not the PNGs that produced the results, what produces results is how dicom, which is the raw data, is handled and preprocessed

Yes, we used .nii files for 3D segmentation model

@harshitsheoran

If a patient has 1000 slices, only some parts will have extravasation, but if you cut it with 96 equidistant slices, there will be at least 10 volumes and have more parts without extravasation, so I wonder if you labeled all volumes (10 volumes in this case) as extravasation and trained the model.
Image-level labels for extravasation and bowel are provided in the training data.

Congratulations! You have done an excellent job.
However, I still have 2 questions.

Question 1:
When you train the extravasation model, how do you obtain the segmentation head label? I'm asking because the dataset only provides image-level information for extravasation.
Is it set like this: If the image indicates a true extravasation injury, is the segmentation training label set to all 1s? If not, is it set to all 0s?

Question 2:
In your GitHub code, the criterion uses nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() directly without any weights. However, during inference, you added the weight as a post-process. Have you tried using a weighted BCEWithLogitsLoss?

Answer 1
Segmentation head segments liver-kidney-spleen, and not extravasation, it is like an auxiliary guidance which does not directly helps extravasation

Answer 2
Yes, we did try weighted BCE loss, in our experiments, it did not help model converge, one reason for this could be our sampling, in our GitHub code, you can see that we are sampling injured and non-injured patients equally
Thank you very much！

Congratulations and thanks for sharing! For beginners like me, could you explain why using 32 equidistant slices and 3 adjacent slices is better than stacking 96 slices in the same channel? You also employed this technique in the cervical challenge.

Thanks @nathanbanaste It was more up to the experimentation. One major downside of using a single channel and 96 slices would be a large increase in computation time as we are passing 3x num images to the encoder. Performance-wise, we tried channels 1, 3, 5, 6, out of these 3 & 5 worked the best for us.

What i meant was that you used 32,3,image_size,image_size for input shape.
So you say that this input shape 32,3,img_size,img_size is less computation than 96,img_size,img_size (with same batch_size)?
Yes, (2, 32, 3, 384, 384) is much less compute than (2, 96, 1, 384, 384), shape being (batch_size, n_slices, n_channels, img_size, img_size)
Thanks for providing us your solution
